newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - May 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - May 7.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Wednesday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* In tobacco industry settlement talks, cigarette makers proposed limits for smokers seeking industry compensation, according to people involved in the talks.
* Shares of Bre-X Minerals collapsed on news the company's purported massive gold find was a hoax.
* Britian's newly-elected Labour government raised base interest rates by 0.25 percent and moved towards making the Bank of England an independent central bank.
* In March, factory orders fell 1.6 percent, the largest decline in seven months.
* The Dow Jones industrial average closed up 10.83 points at 7,225.32.
* The U.S. Federal Trade Commission is probing compact disk prices and has asked large recording companies about the enforcement of pricing policies.
* Viacom is trying to emphasize Blockbuster's core video business once again, after its former head attempted to move the company into retail.
* Fluor said it expected to post a net loss of about $70 million for its second quarter because of $140 million in pre-tax one-time charges.
* Credit Suisse First Boston paid 33 former investment bankers from its defunct munibond operation a total of $4 million in a bonus dispute.
* GTE agreed to pay $616 million to buy Internet service provider BBN and said it planned to increase capital spending at least $2 billion over four years.
* Aetna and Oxford Health reported strong operating earnings in the quarter and their shares rose.
* Vencor said it bid $639 million for Transitional Hospitals after Transition said it agreed to be purchased by another company for $564.5 million.
* Nine West said the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission was probing the company's methods of booking revenues.

* Heard on the Street: Investors in stocks of high-tech and pharmaceutical companies, beware. A study warns that a growing number of companies are using an obscure accounting rule that some critics say can inflate subsequent earnings artificially.
* Credit markets: In the wake of a lackluster auction of three-year notes, Treasury prices were moderately lower yesterday, halting a six-day run of consecutively higher closes.
